newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll sees French centre-right winning election.
newsitem.headline: Poll sees French centre-right winning election.

text.p: An opinion poll released on Tuesday saw France's centre-right government retaining a comfortable majority over the left-wing opposition in the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election.
The CSA survey said the ruling centre-right coalition could win 317 National Assembly seats, 80 more than the combined left's 237.

The survey of 1,023 registered voters carried out on Monday and Tuesday confirmed a trend towards a comfortable conservative victory seen in recent polls, but saw both the centre-right and the main opposition Socialist party slightly losing steam.
It said the ruling coalition could poll 39.5 percent of the votes, down from 40.5 percent a week ago.
The Socialists dipped to 28 percent from 30 and were seen winning 215 seats, with their Communist allies advancing to 10.5 percent from 10 and winning 22 seats.
Ecologists rose to seven percent from 4.5 while the far-right National Front was stable at 13.5 percent, winning one seat.
A narrow majority of 43 percent to 41 said power-sharing between conservative President Jacques Chirac and a left-wing prime minister would be harmful for the country.

If the centre-right retained power, Gaullist ex-National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a former anti-Maastricht campaigner, topped the list of preferred prime ministers with 23 percent, ahead of fellow-Gaullist ex-premier Edouard Balladur with 21 percent.
Ultra-liberal Alain Madelin was third with 11 percent and Prime Minister Alain Juppe fourth with eight percent.
